name: Social facilitation
statement: Having other people present speeds up simple, well-practised performance and degrades performance on complex tasks.
meaning: The claim has two halves pointing opposite ways. An audience or a co-worker strengthens whatever response is already dominant, so a well-practised task gets faster while a task whose dominant response is the wrong one gets worse. Zajonc set that out in 1965 by borrowing Hull and Spence's behaviour theory: presence raises generalised drive, drive energises the dominant habit, and task complexity decides whether that habit is the right answer. Rival accounts keep the pattern and change the cause. Cottrell argued that presence alone is not enough and that the performer must expect to be judged. Sanders, Baron and Moore argued that the other person is a distraction, and that conflict between attending to them and attending to the task is what produces the drive. The three accounts agree on almost every prediction, which is why they have outlived the attempts to separate them.

origin.note: Triplett studied competition and pacemaking, not social facilitation, and never used the term. McHugh and colleagues date the name to Floyd Allport in 1920, two decades later. Gordon Allport's 1954 handbook chapter is what installed Triplett as the first social psychology experiment, and Stroebe argues that attribution is wrong on every count.

evidence: Triplett started from bicycle records. Official League of American Wheelmen figures to the close of the 1897 season put paced competition races ahead of paced races against time by an average of 5.15 seconds per mile up to 25 miles. His laboratory version had children turn a fishing reel until a small flag had made four circuits of a four-metre course. Records were taken from nearly 225 people of all ages, and every table in the paper rests on 40 children, split into two groups of 20 running different orders of alone and competition trials. Triplett sorted them by eye into 20 stimulated positively, 10 overstimulated and slower in competition, and 10 barely affected. He reported probable errors and no significance test, because the modern ones did not exist. His conclusion was that the bodily presence of another contestant "serves to liberate latent energy not ordinarily available". Zajonc, Heingartner and Herman later moved the question to an animal with no reputation to protect. Their Experiment 1 ran 72 adult female Blatta orientalis cockroaches away from a floodlight, down a straight runway or through a maze, alone or in company. Each roach ran ten trials and its median time was the score. Company took two forms, coaction and an audience of roaches held in boxes whose air holes lined up with holes in the walls of the apparatus. The coaction comparison had 8 roaches per cell and the audience comparison 10. Average median runway times fell from 62.65 seconds alone to 39.30 seconds with an audience, while maze times rose from 221.35 to 296.64. The paper pooled coaction and audience into a social condition and reported a significant conditions by tasks interaction on running time, df = 1/64, p < 0.01. Maze times got worse in company and runway times got better. The quantitative record is Bond and Titus, who pooled 241 studies, 23,970 subjects and 742 separate effects. Presence made simple performance faster, d = 0.32 across 154 effects, and complex performance slower, d = -0.20 across 54. It made complex work less accurate, d = -0.36 across 147 effects, the largest mean effect in the analysis. It barely touched the accuracy of simple work, d = 0.11 across 112 effects.

examples.tag: The scales played for a listener
examples.text: A pianist runs through scales she has practised for years and plays them faster with someone in the room. She then tries a piece learned that week and fumbles passages she managed alone.

A cook plates the dish she has made a thousand times more quickly with the room watching, and makes more errors on the special she has cooked twice. Presence strengthens whatever response is already the habit.

examples.tag: Typing up notes against writing a hard paragraph
examples.text: In an open office the routine typing goes faster with colleagues nearby, and the difficult paragraph goes worse. The complexity of the task, not the worker's mood, decides which way the presence of others pushes.

replication.headline: Two preregistered direct replications came out on opposite sides: 445 children reproduced Triplett's speed-up in company, while the cockroach experiment produced the impairment half of the effect and no trace of the facilitation half.
replication.detail: McHugh and colleagues rebuilt Triplett's apparatus and ran Irish schoolchildren aged 7 to 13 in a registered report. They recruited 474 in 240 dyads, dropped 29 whose data were unusable, and analysed 445, having powered the study in advance to detect f-squared = 0.02 with 400. Alone they took 58.4 seconds, SD 13.5; together 55.0 seconds, SD 11.8; F(1, 444) = 133.73, p < 0.001. The effect survived controls for trial order and practice, and was stronger for girls, b = -4.07, than for boys, b = -2.75. It did not survive every specification: with covariates and interactions in the right-handed-only sample, condition was no longer significant. The authors also state plainly that their design cannot separate social facilitation from competition. Halfmann, Bredehöft and Häusser ran a preregistered direct replication of the cockroach study as a 2 by 2 of audience and task difficulty, tripling the original's cell sizes. They collected until 120 roaches had at least two successful trials, and 17 more were excluded for failing that criterion. Roaches were slower with an audience, mean 164.59 seconds against 49.90 alone, F(1, 116) = 55.58, p < 0.001, partial eta-squared 0.32. The maze took longer than the runway, 137.48 seconds against 77.00, F(1, 116) = 15.45, p < 0.001, partial eta-squared 0.12. The audience slowed both tasks, the complex one at t(58) = -4.00, d = -1.00, as predicted, and the simple one at t(58) = -9.37, d = -2.41, against prediction. The audience by difficulty interaction that the original had never tested statistically did not appear, F(1, 116) = 0.02, p = 0.882, with a Bayes factor of 3.88 for the null. Their summary is that they replicated the social-inhibition effect and found no evidence for a social-facilitation effect. Modern pooling on human motor tasks lands in the same divided place. Van Meurs, Greve and Strauss reviewed 82 studies and 7,008 participants, and the 28 studies with usable data, 1,907 participants and 47 effects, gave an overall d = 0.29, 95% CI [0.03, 0.55], p = 0.030, with I-squared of 87%. Splitting by task, condition-based work resting on strength, speed and endurance was facilitated, d = 0.84, 95% CI [0.46, 1.23] across 16 effects. Coordination under precision pressure gave d = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.88, 0.95] across 14, coordination under time pressure d = 0.12, 95% CI [-1.01, 1.26] across 5, and mixed tasks d = -0.05, 95% CI [-1.07, 0.97] across 12. Of the four, only the condition-based estimate excluded zero.

study.cite: McHugh, C., Griffin, S. M., Kinsella, E. L., Quayle, M., Strunz, B., & Muldoon, O. T. (2025). A replication of Triplett's 'social facilitation experiment'. Scientific Reports, 15, 40366.

limits: The pooled effects are small enough that the label oversells them. Bond and Titus put the presence of others at 0.3% to 3% of the variance in a typical experiment. Their largest effect, the impairment of complex accuracy, accounts for 3.1% of between-subjects variance, and the median effect for 1.3%. The facilitation of simple accuracy accounts for 0.30%, and it is fragile: nearly 40% of the reported effects run the other way, and 194 unreported null results would sink it to non-significance. Between 17.4% and 42.6% of effects point against the mean, depending on the measure. The control condition is also weaker than it sounds. In only 100 of the 241 studies did the authors state that the experimenter had left the room. An experimenter shared the room with the supposedly alone subject in 96 studies, and in 52 of those the subject could see the experimenter. Evaluation apprehension fares badly in the same data. Bond and Titus report that evaluation potential does not reliably magnify the social effect on performance quantity, on performance quality or on physiology during simple tasks, which cuts against Cottrell's account rather than Zajonc's. Their one exception is physiological: evaluative others raise a complex performer's arousal while non-evaluative others lower it, p < 0.05. Van Meurs and colleagues could use only 28 of their 82 reviewed studies in the meta-analysis, and their heterogeneity was 87%. Four sources were not obtained. Strube's reanalysis of Triplett's data is paywalled at the publisher and at the Scholarly Publishing Collective, whose page also returns a bot challenge, so his numbers are quoted here as McHugh and colleagues report them, with their page citations, and his own abstract is read from PubMed. Zajonc's 1965 Science article was not obtained either, and the drive account above is taken from the expositions in Bond and Titus and in Halfmann and colleagues. Cottrell and colleagues' 1968 paper is paywalled at the publisher, and the copy at Academia.edu returns a bot challenge. Haines and Vaughan's 1979 paper is paywalled at Wiley, whose abstract page returns a bot challenge, and neither PubMed, Crossref nor Semantic Scholar carries its abstract. Searches on 21 September 2026 covered Crossref, PubMed, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, CORE, OSF, the Groningen and Frankfurt repositories and web search.
misreadings: Triplett is not the founding experiment, and his own data do not carry the finding. Haines and Vaughan questioned the 1898 date in 1979, and McHugh and colleagues cite them for the claim that the first-experiment status is contested. Stroebe's abstract is blunter: not the first social psychology study, not even the first on social facilitation, the task described wrongly in textbooks, and the evidence overstated. Strube reanalysed the original records with modern tests and reports in his abstract that very little evidence existed for social facilitation of the simple task Triplett used. As McHugh and colleagues report it, the between-subjects comparisons ran the right way but were not significant, the within-subject analyses showed little, and only averaging the alone and competition trials produced a marginal effect, which Strube summarised as evidence that "can be coaxed from the data" giving "barely a statistical hint of the social facilitation of performance to which his experiment has been credited". The size of the effect is the second misreading. Cooper and Findley, quoted by Bond and Titus, found social psychology textbooks presenting a mean effect of d = 1.19, or 26.1% of the variance in a typical experiment, against the 0.3% to 3% their own pooling gives. The third is the mechanism. Triplett's children raced each other and Zajonc's theory is about presence, so a study of competing co-actors is often read as evidence about being watched, and McHugh and colleagues say their own replication cannot tell the two apart.

Halfmann, E., Bredehöft, J., & Häusser, J. A. (2020). Replicating roaches: A preregistered direct replication of Zajonc, Heingartner, and Herman's (1969) social-facilitation study. Psychological Science, 31(3), 332-337. Full text read from the Goethe University Frankfurt deposit, which OpenAlex labels a submitted version and which is the typeset article of record.

van Meurs, E., Greve, J., & Strauss, B. (2024). Moving in the presence of others: A systematic review and meta-analysis on social facilitation. International Review of Sport and Exercise Psychology, 17(2), 980-1012. Figures read from the authors' postprint, which says on its first page that it is not the version of record. The version of record is paywalled at Taylor and Francis, so the two could not be compared.

Perez Neider, D., Fuse, M., & Suri, G. (2019). Cockroaches, performance, and an audience: Reexamining social facilitation 50 years later. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 85, 103851. The copy read is the authors' manuscript, whose abstract matches the published one word for word. It proposes a replication and reports no results. Its power analysis puts the original interaction at eta-squared = 0.025, a figure the authors computed rather than one Zajonc and colleagues printed.

Stroebe, W. (2012). The truth about Triplett (1898), but nobody seems to care. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 7(1), 54-57. Abstract read at PubMed on 21 September 2026. OpenAlex and Unpaywall list the Groningen repository deposit as an open published version, and the PDF that deposit links returns a Cloudflare bot challenge rather than a paywall, so the full text is unread.

Strube, M. J. (2005). What did Triplett really find? A contemporary analysis of the first experiment in social psychology. The American Journal of Psychology, 118(2), 271-286. Abstract read at PubMed and at the Washington University research profile. The full text is paywalled, and the Scholarly Publishing Collective page for it returns a bot challenge, so the reanalysis is quoted here as McHugh and colleagues report it, with their page citations.

Haines, H., & Vaughan, G. M. (1979). Was 1898 a 'great date' in the history of experimental social psychology? Journal of the History of the Behavioral Sciences, 15(4), 323-332. Not obtained. Wiley's abstract page returns a bot challenge, and PubMed, Crossref and Semantic Scholar hold the record without an abstract. Cited here only as the paper McHugh and colleagues name for the contested origin date.

Zajonc, R. B. (1965). Social facilitation. Science, 149(3681), 269-274. Not obtained. Science's own page returns a 403, Unpaywall lists no open copy, and searches of OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and the web found none. The drive account is summarised here from the expositions in Bond and Titus and in Halfmann and colleagues.

Zajonc, R. B., Heingartner, A., & Herman, E. M. (1969). Social enhancement and impairment of performance in the cockroach. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 13(2), 83-92. Full text read from the scanned copy at Fermat's Library, whose optical character recognition renders the analysis-of-variance table poorly, so no F value is quoted from it.

Cottrell, N. B., Wack, D. L., Sekerak, G. J., & Rittle, R. H. (1968). Social facilitation of dominant responses by the presence of an audience and the mere presence of others. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 9(3), 245-250. Named as the evaluation-apprehension source Bond and Titus test against.
